name: Error management theory
statement: Error management theory holds that selection biased judgement under uncertainty towards the cheaper mistake, so some errors are design features rather than flaws.
meaning: This is a framework, not a finding. It says that when a judgement can go wrong in two directions and one direction cost more over evolutionary time, the deciding mechanism should lean towards the cheaper error. A smoke alarm is the standard illustration: missed fires cost more than false alarms, so the alarm is set to cry wolf. Haselton and Buss applied the logic to reading the opposite sex and derived two predictions. Men should overperceive women's sexual interest, because a missed opportunity cost an ancestral man more than a wasted approach. Women should underperceive men's intent to commit, because trusting a man who leaves cost an ancestral woman more than waiting too long. The same logic has been attached to hearing approaching sounds, judging heights and detecting agents. Because the content of any prediction lives in an assumed cost matrix, the framework's record has to be read prediction by prediction. Nothing follows from the theory until somebody states which error was dearer, and that premise is rarely measured.

origin.who: Martie G. Haselton and David M. Buss
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: The paper names the theory and reports two questionnaire studies of American undergraduates, 217 in Study 1 and 289 in Study 2. Men's overperception of women's sexual intent was already an established finding it set out to explain, credited in the text to Abbey's work from 1982 onwards. The new prediction was women's commitment scepticism.

evidence:
Study 1 asked 113 men and 104 women to rate three statements about commitment and eight behaviours for sexual interest. Women rated men's commitment avoidance higher, 4.52 against men's own 3.96 on a seven-point scale, F(1, 213) = 10.63, p < .01. Ratings of women's commitment did not differ by sex of rater. The sexual-intent items produced no interaction at all, only a main effect of rater: men gave higher ratings than women, 3.70 against 3.39, F(1, 211) = 6.73, p = .01. The authors say this may mean men's overperception extends to targets of both sexes.

Study 2 used 15 dating cues and added self-perception as a second criterion. Women judged men's commitment intent lower than men judged their own, 1.21 against 1.65, F(1, 279) = 31.58, p < .001. Men judged women's sexual intent higher than women judged themselves, 1.02 against 0.13, F(1, 270) = 28.84, p < .001. Women also rated men's sexual intent above men's self-ratings, 1.42 against 1.10, F(1, 273) = 2.40, p = .02, which the paper says contradicts a general oversexualisation account. The claim of a bias rests on a cross-sex rating falling outside both criterion measures, and men's perception of women's sexual intent was the case that did so.

The sibling test used 131 eligible participants. Men rated their sisters' sexual intent at -1.03 against -0.02 for other women, F(1, 57) = 23.62, p < .001. Women, for whom no prediction had been made, rated their brothers at -0.50 against 1.37 for other men, F(1, 70) = 111.94, p < .001.

Haselton's 2003 survey moved the question to remembered events, asking people how often the opposite sex had misread them. Its design is described here from Bendixen's account rather than from the paper itself, which was not opened. Henningsen and Henningsen put 111 stranger dyads into face-to-face conversation and found support with boundary conditions, including that people project their own level of interest onto a partner.

Outside mating, the auditory looming bias is the most cited case. Neuhoff, Planisek and Seifritz report that both sexes underestimate the time to arrival of approaching sounds, that the bias is stronger in women, and that no sex difference appears for receding sounds. Merz and colleagues, summarising the earlier work, state that looming sounds are heard as changing more sharply than matched receding sounds and are expected to arrive sooner than they do. Baumgartner and colleagues reproduced a looming asymmetry using spectral cues at constant intensity, which answers the objection that the effect was about loudness rather than distance.

replication.headline: The survey pattern behind the sexual overperception bias replicates in Norway and Japan, and the reading of it as an evolved perceptual bias in men has not survived larger and better-controlled tests.
replication.detail:
Bendixen ran a direct replication of Haselton's 2003 survey on 308 Norwegian students, 181 women and 127 men, chosen because Norway is more gender-equal than the United States. Over their lifetimes 88.3% of women reported having been sexually overperceived against 39.4% underperceived, while for men the two figures were 70.6% and 74.6%. For the past year, women reported overperception far more often than underperception, t(180) = 10.76, p < .001, d = 0.94, and the same contrast in men was much smaller, t(126) = 3.76, p < .001, d = 0.29. Bendixen estimates the corresponding figures in Haselton's original at d = 0.80 for women and d = 0.16 for men, using Cortina and Nouri's formula applied to the original's reported statistics. Those two numbers are Bendixen's calculation, not Haselton's, and are quoted here as such. Hiraishi, Murasaki, Okuda and Yamate replicated the pattern in a Japanese undergraduate sample.

What those surveys measure is how often people say they were misread. Studies that compare a perceiver's judgement with a target's own report have gone the other way. Lee, Sidari, Murphy, Sherlock and Zietsch ran 1,226 speed daters, 586 men and 640 women. Men overperceived and women underperceived, and the sex difference became negligible once the raters' sociosexual orientation and their tendency to project their own interest onto partners were entered as mediators. The authors state this challenges the idea that the sex difference is a specialised adaptation. Henningsen and Henningsen had already found the projection effect in 111 dyads in 2010.

Perilloux and Kurzban attacked the inference rather than the data. Across three studies they reproduced the sex difference, showed men held to their ratings when paid for accuracy, and showed women think other women understate their intentions. Their conclusion is that men may be reading women correctly and managing error through biased behaviour instead of biased belief. Murray, Murphy, von Hippel, Trivers and Haselton replied with a preregistered test of the competing predictions and concluded that men do overestimate. Perilloux and Kurzban published a reply in the same issue. None of the three papers could be read beyond its title and record, and their contents are described here from the 2015 abstract and from the titles of the 2017 exchange.

Brandner, Pohlman and Brase re-analysed the measurement itself with signal detection theory. Sensitivity to interest and disinterest signals, not a standing bias towards seeing interest, drove what people reported, and cues of interest were underperceived overall. The apparent male bias came from error management's use of difference scores, which hide where each sex starts.

The auditory prediction has now failed a direct test. Merz and colleagues used a probe comparison task from the representational momentum literature to ask where a changing sound is heard to end. The adaptive account predicts a forward shift for approaching sounds. Every condition in both experiments shifted backwards, and there was no effect of intensity change direction in Experiment 1, F(1, 29) = 0.91, p = .347. Complex tones in Experiment 2 shifted further backwards than pure tones, F(1, 60) = 4.51, p = .038, again against prediction.

Sex-specificity fares worst of all. In a preregistered study of 710 adults from Buss's own laboratory, Baca, Costello, Hahnel-Peeters, Thomas, Schmitt and Buss found that men overestimated women's desire for sexual variety, and that women showed the same bias about men, and that both sexes overestimated their own sex too.

study.cite: Bendixen, M. (2014). Evidence of systematic bias in sexual over- and underperception of naturally occurring events: A direct replication of Haselton (2003) in a more gender-equal culture. Evolutionary Psychology, 12(5), 1004-1021.

limits:
The structured effect size is one contrast from one replication: women's reported frequency of being overperceived against being underperceived over the past year. It is not a measure of anyone's perceptual accuracy, and it does not summarise the theory. No effect size is given for the original studies, because Haselton and Buss report F tests and condition means and no standardised effect, and because the 2003 survey was not obtainable. Bendixen's estimates of the original's effect sizes are his arithmetic on the original's statistics and are reported on this page as his.

Several papers were located but not read. Haselton's 2003 article, the 2017 exchange between Murray and colleagues and Perilloux and Kurzban, Johnson, Blumstein, Fowler and Haselton's 2013 review in Trends in Ecology and Evolution, and Neuhoff's 1998 and 2001 papers are all paywalled, and searches of Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall and the authors' university pages turned up no readable copy. What the 1998 and 2001 experiments found is stated here on Merz and colleagues' summary of them. La France, Henningsen, Oates and Shaw published meta-analyses of sex differences in perceptions of flirtatiousness, seductiveness and promiscuousness in Communication Monographs in 2009, which Haselton and Galperin cite as support. Its effect sizes could not be obtained from any source reached, so no figure from it appears here.

No multi-site replication, registered replication report or meta-analysis of error management theory as such was found. The search covered Crossref, Europe PMC, PubMed, Semantic Scholar and Unpaywall. Preregistration exists at the level of individual studies: Murray and colleagues in 2017, Baca and colleagues in 2026.

The deeper limit is that most predictions attributed to the theory have never been tested. Height overestimation, snake detection, food aversion, infidelity detection and interpersonal threat all appear in review chapters under the error management heading, and this entry examined only cross-sex inference and auditory looming.

McKay and Efferson argue that the theory is vague about what a bias is, that it is unclear whether the cognitive biases it defends are anything more than behavioural biases, and that on that reading it reduces to expected utility theory. Their own proposal is that departures from Bayesian belief can be adaptive when they produce error-avoiding behaviour. Al-Shawaf, writing from inside the framework, shows that the sex-specific framing does not follow from it: what drives a bias is the cost matrix, so a father assessing his daughter's suitor should show commitment scepticism and a mother assessing her son's prospects should show sexual overperception. He calls these the sceptical dad and encouraging mom hypotheses and notes that they are untested. If a cost matrix can be assigned after the data arrive, the framework will fit any result.
misreadings:
The commonest error is to treat error management theory as a single effect with a single replication record. It is a way of generating hypotheses. Men's overperception of women's sexual intent was an established finding before the theory arrived, and the theory's own novel prediction was women's commitment scepticism, which has been tested far less.

The second is to cite Study 1 as evidence that men specifically overperceive women. It found no interaction between sex of rater and sex of target on the sexual-intent items. Men rated men as more sexually interested as well, and the paper says so. Only Study 2, with self-report as a second criterion, isolates the cross-sex effect.

The third is the sister correction. Men did rate their sisters far below other women, which is what was predicted. Women rated their brothers far below other men on a comparison for which no prediction had been made, and by a larger margin. A result that appears equally in the condition with no hypothesis attached is weak support for the hypothesis.

The fourth is to read the survey replications as evidence about perception. Bendixen and Hiraishi asked people how often the opposite sex had misjudged them. Women say it happens often and men say it rarely happens in that direction. Whether men's judgements are wrong is a separate question, and the studies that ask it, by comparing a rating against the target's own report, are where the sex difference thins out.

The fifth is to assume a bias in behaviour requires a bias in belief. Perilloux and Kurzban's position is that men may perceive accurately and act on low-probability chances anyway, which is error management working through action. Brandner and colleagues make the measurement version of the same point: difference scores cannot separate sensitivity from criterion, and when signal detection theory separates them, sensitivity does the work.

The entry on agent detection rests on the same asymmetric-cost argument, that a false alarm is cheaper than a missed predator, and its record is worth comparing. There the framing prediction failed directly, since threat did not raise agent detection and the measured criterion was conservative. Here the target phenomenon is real and the argument about what causes it is unsettled. A cost asymmetry that sounds obvious has now twice failed to deliver the perceptual bias it was supposed to imply.
